newsitem.title: USA: Big alumina expansion in Jamaica doubtful-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Big alumina expansion in Jamaica doubtful-analysts.

text.p: Jamaica's alumina industry is unlikely to see any major expansions soon, delegates at Metal Bulletin's Bauxite and Alumina seminar were told.
Analyst Mark Fraser of CRU International told a panel discussion that apart from a small expansion of about 200,000 tonnes a year at the Clarendon plant, little else was expected.
Some two tonnes of alumina are used to make one tonne of aluminum metal.

Jamaica has been looking to expand existing alumina plants and build new ones such as the North Coast Trelawny project in a bid to halt the relative decline of the industry as output from low cost producers in Australia rises steadily.
Alumina and bauxite generated some US$713.2 million in gross earnings in 1995, and a similar figure was expected in 1996.
Alumina plants are fairly old in Jamaica and the industry has been shedding staff in the past year in a bid to improve efficiency.
Julian Kettle of Brook Hunt consultancy said he did not hold out high hopes for the North Coast alumina project.
Owners of existing alumina plants in Jamaica knew that current capacity was not being fully used and did not want to become involved in expansions at the moment, Kettle added.

Some analyst saw potential for expansion at the Alpart plant, but Peter McIntosh of Kaiser Aluminum Corp, which owns 65 percent of Alpart, said capacity was underused and issues such as costs remained to be solved.
"Cost issues of operating in Jamaica have to be resolved before we see commitment for expansion," McIntosh said.

Alpart has had a "chequered history", McIntosh said, but power issues appeared to have been dealt with. Output was now close to design capacity and this year will be "better than at any stage in the past".
Disrupted power supplies pushed up operating costs at the plant last year, Kaiser has said.
